Independent support from early manuscripts, ancient versions, transcriptions, parallel passages, or another demonstrable reading tradition materially strengthens the case; the burden is heavier when the Masoretic reading is natural, coherent, and broadly corroborated.","required_support":["Compatibility with the transmitted consonantal text, including written vowel letters","A morphologically and syntactically valid construction appropriate to the language, period, and genre","Lexically attested usage rather than a merely imaginable assignment of vowels or meaning","Coherence with the immediate discourse and broader literary context","Careful comparison with Ketiv/Qere, parallel passages, early manuscripts, ancient translations, and transcriptions where available","Distinction between evidence for alternate vocalization and evidence for a different consonantal text","An account of exceptional grammar, orthography, semantic usage, or required emendation","An explanation of why the alternate reading is preferable or plausibly competitive with the received pointing"],"core_rule":"The transmitted consonantal letters, including any written vowel letters, are the primary written textual datum. They therefore carry a rebuttable presumption, but not automatic veto authority: an alternate vocalization may be admitted only when the consonants permit it and substantial linguistic, contextual, and preferably historical evidence supports it.","strongest_chapter_evidence":["Torah scrolls are transmitted and publicly read without the later Tiberian pointing signs, directly illustrating the distinction between consonantal text and supplied vocalization.","The Tiberian pointing system was graphically fixed centuries after the biblical compositions, so the signs themselves cannot generally be identified with the original written graphemes.","The example חלב illustrates that one consonantal sequence can, in principle, receive materially different vocalizations, making vocalization an interpretive and linguistic question rather than a purely graphic fact.","The chapter expressly requires proposed rereadings to be tested against the letters, occurrences, witnesses, and counterevidence rather than accepted merely because they are possible.","Early manuscripts and ancient translations can preserve evidence relevant to pre-Masoretic textual or reading traditions, although each witness requires critical evaluation."],"unresolved_objections":["The chapter sometimes conflates alternate vocalization of identical consonants with consonantal textual variants. Psalm 22's yod/vav issue is chiefly a consonantal variant, not evidence that vowel points themselves altered the reading.","Psalm 40 and Hebrews 10 do not by themselves establish a mere repointing of identical Hebrew consonants; the Greek reading may reflect a different Vorlage, interpretive translation, or other textual development.","The claim that Qumran manuscripts carry simply 'bare consonants' is imprecise because ancient Hebrew orthography includes written vowel letters, and Qumran texts often employ relatively full orthography.","The New Testament references to synagogue exclusion do not demonstrate that the Masoretic vocalization system was systematically shaped to suppress Christian readings centuries later.","General biblical warnings against human tradition or adding words do not prove that recording vowels as annotations is illicit, nor do they determine the exact evidentiary weight those annotations deserve.","The chapter's polemic against synagogue bias is historically under-supported and unnecessary to its sounder textual distinction between consonants and later pointing.","Ancient translations are indirect witnesses whose divergences may arise from different consonants, translation technique, paraphrase, or interpretation; chronological priority alone does not make them decisive.","The chapter gives insufficient attention to the antiquity, internal coherence, linguistic expertise, and broad corroboration of much of the received Masoretic reading tradition."],"rationale":"The chapter substantially confirms the prior methodological premise: consonants are the primary written datum, while the Masoretic points encode a later recorded reading tradition that deserves weight but cannot alone veto a well-supported alternate vocalization. Its demand that rereadings be constrained by letters and witnesses also agrees with the prior burden of proof. I am only partly persuaded by the chapter as an argument because several flagship examples concern consonantal variants rather than repointing, and its claims of anti-Christian Masoretic bias exceed the evidence presented. Those defects do not defeat the core rule, but neither do they justify reducing the received pointing from a rebuttable presumption to mere unprivileged evidence.","confidence":"HIGH"}
